openers.title: The Citation to Nowhere
openers.prompt: An AI research brief says: "Teens who study with music score 40% higher on memory tests (Harlow & Min, 2021, Journal of Adolescent Learning Science, vol. 14)." It looks polished and specific. Fact or fake?
options: Can't tell until I trace it
openers.teacher: Students vote with fingers, then pairs list the exact steps they would take to trace the citation. Ask: "What would count as proof that this study exists and says this?"
openers.answer: Treat it as fake until traced. The authors, journal, and 40% figure were invented for this opener, which is exactly what a hallucinated citation looks like: real-sounding names, a volume number, a neat statistic. Search for the article itself, confirm the journal exists, and read what the study actually found.
openers.lookFor: Students describe concrete tracing steps (search the title and authors, find the journal, read the abstract) rather than judging by how professional it looks.
openers.next: Students will trace every claim and citation in a full AI research brief.

openers.title: The Voicemail From Dana
openers.prompt: The night before the Riverton mayoral election, a voicemail spreads in group chats. It sounds exactly like candidate Dana Whitfield: "Because of the storm, voting for my supporters has moved to Wednesday." Your cousin asks if they should forward it.
openers.teacher: Students go to three corners and each corner explains its reasoning in one sentence. Ask: "Where would you go to confirm when and where voting happens?"
openers.answer: Don't forward it, and check the official election office. A familiar voice is no longer proof, since voices can be cloned from short clips. Election dates don't move for one candidate's supporters, and the timing (the night before) is a classic pressure tactic.
openers.lookFor: Students name an official source to check and explain why a convincing voice is not evidence.
openers.next: Student newsroom teams will race a deadline to sort real, synthetic, and unconfirmed election tips.

openers.title: One Honest Sentence
openers.prompt: Jaylen used an AI chatbot to brainstorm three possible thesis statements for a history essay, picked one, rewrote it, and wrote the whole essay himself. His teacher allows AI for brainstorming if you disclose it. Write the one-sentence disclosure Jaylen should put at the end.
openers.teacher: Students write for two minutes, then trade with a partner who checks: does it say what tool type, what it did, and what Jaylen did himself? Ask: "What would make a disclosure feel honest instead of like a loophole?"
openers.answer: A strong example: "I used an AI chatbot to brainstorm three possible thesis statements; I chose and revised one, and the research, argument, and writing are my own."
openers.lookFor: Disclosures name what the AI did and what the student did, specifically enough that a reader could picture the process.
openers.next: Students will sort academic integrity dilemmas across courses and write process logs they would stand behind.

openers.title: Free App or Private App?
openers.prompt: Would you rather use StudyNest AI, which is free but reads every document in your cloud drive to "personalize your help," or QuietNotes, which costs a few dollars a month and says it deletes your files after each session?
openers.teacher: Students move to one side of the room, then talk across the line with someone who chose differently. Ask: "What would you need to read or change before trusting either one?"
openers.answer: Both are fictional, and both claims need checking. Free tools often pay for themselves with your data, while a paid tool's promise is only as good as its privacy policy. Good questions: what is collected, who it is shared with, how long it is kept, and whether you can turn it off or delete it.
openers.lookFor: Students name at least one thing they would look for in a privacy policy or settings, not just price.
openers.next: Teams will read a mock AI study app's privacy policy like investigators and map where their data could go.

openers.title: The SoleVault Storefront
openers.prompt: Picture an online store called SoleVault Outlet: limited sneakers at 80% off, a timer counting down from 9:59, hundreds of five-star reviews all posted the same week, and a checkout page that only accepts gift cards or a payment app transfer. What do you notice, and what would you check, in order?
openers.teacher: Pairs list the red flags, then put their checks in the order they would do them. Ask: "Which single clue would make you walk away, even if everything else looked fine?"
openers.answer: The biggest clue is the payment method: gift cards and direct transfers are hard or impossible to reverse. The countdown creates pressure, the too-good price is a lure, and a burst of same-week reviews can be fake or AI-written. A careful order: look up the store's name plus "scam" or "reviews," check its contact and return info, and pay only with a method that offers protection.
openers.lookFor: Students put checks in a logical sequence and single out the payment method as the deciding clue.
openers.next: Students will practice checking the storefront, deal, reviews, and payment before they buy, and what to do if something goes wrong.

openers.title: Redesign One Feature
openers.prompt: Pick one feature of a social app: infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks, or like counts. With a partner, explain what it is designed to make you do, then redesign it so it serves people instead of engagement.
openers.teacher: Pairs choose one feature, talk for four minutes, and sketch the redesign in one sentence or a quick drawing. Share three. Ask: "Would the company that makes the app want your version? Why or why not?"
openers.answer: Examples: scroll that pauses with a "you're caught up" message, autoplay that is off by default, streaks that can be paused without penalty, like counts only the poster sees. The tension is that these redesigns may reduce time on the app, which is what many apps are built to increase.
openers.lookFor: Redesigns name the behavior the original feature encourages and change the feature to support a different goal.
openers.next: Students will dissect a fictional social app's design features and redesign the whole feed.

openers.title: Who Owns the Winner?
openers.prompt: Priya typed a detailed prompt into an image generator, picked the best of 30 results, edited the colors, and won the Lakeview art contest. Who deserves the most credit for the image?
options: The company that made the tool
The artists whose work trained it
openers.teacher: Students go to four corners, then each corner sends one speaker to make its best case in 30 seconds. Ask: "Did anyone hear an argument from another corner that made them want to move?"
openers.answer: This is an open question; courts, contests, and schools are still working it out. Strong answers weigh Priya's choices, the tool's role, and the artists whose work trained the model, and they notice that the contest's own rules and honest disclosure matter a lot.
openers.lookFor: Students restate another corner's argument fairly before responding, and some students change corners.
openers.next: Students will argue both sides of AI training and credit in a structured academic controversy.

openers.title: Coach or Crutch?
openers.prompt: Big chemistry test tomorrow. Would you rather use an AI that gives you correct answers to the practice problems instantly, or one that only asks you questions and hints until you solve them yourself?
openers.teacher: Students show a thumb up for instant answers, thumb down for hints, then write one line: which would actually help them on the test, and why. Ask: "What does your choice say about how you learn best?"
openers.answer: Instant answers feel faster, but the test asks you to solve problems without help, so practicing the solving is what transfers. Hints can be slower and more frustrating, which is often a sign your brain is doing the work. A mix can work: try first, then check.
openers.lookFor: Students connect their choice to what the test will actually require and to their own learning habits.
openers.next: Students will write custom instructions that turn a chatbot into a coach that makes them think.

openers.title: Draft the Rule
openers.prompt: Your school board asks students for one sentence to include in the new AI-use policy. With a partner, draft that sentence, then ask: who might be left out or hurt by it?
openers.teacher: Pairs draft for three minutes, then join another pair to test each sentence against "who might be left out?" Collect the best sentences on the board. Ask: "What evidence would convince adults your rule works?"
openers.lookFor: Draft rules are specific and enforceable, and pairs name a group who might be affected, such as students without home internet or students who use assistive tools.
openers.next: Student teams will research, draft, and pitch a full AI and technology-use policy to a mock board.

openers.title: FocusFuel Gummies
openers.prompt: A fitness influencer, Coach Rhys, posts: "FocusFuel gummies boost your memory 300% before exams. Doctors don't want you to know this. Link in bio for 20% off!" Fact or fake?
openers.teacher: Students vote with fingers, then pairs list what they would search to read laterally about Coach Rhys and FocusFuel. Ask: "Who makes money if you believe this?"
openers.answer: Treat it as fake. FocusFuel, Coach Rhys, and the 300% figure are invented for this opener, and the post shows classic warning signs: a huge number with no source, a "doctors don't want you to know" hook, and a discount link that pays the poster. Reading laterally means leaving the post to see what independent, qualified sources say, and asking a trusted adult or clinician before taking any supplement.
openers.lookFor: Students name the sales motive and describe leaving the post to check independent sources instead of reading the influencer's own page.
openers.next: Students will check influencer clips, ads, forum posts, and a chatbot answer about wellness.

openers.title: The Fourth Teammate
openers.prompt: Your team of three is making a short documentary, and AI is your "fourth teammate." Sort these jobs: brainstorm interview questions, choose whose story to tell, write captions for accessibility, decide the film's main message, suggest music, fact-check a statistic.
openers.teacher: Groups sort the jobs on a whiteboard in three columns, then compare with another group. Ask: "Which job did you disagree about, and what would settle it?"
openers.answer: Choosing whose story to tell and the main message are human judgment calls. AI can help brainstorm questions or draft captions that people then check. Fact-checking can't be handed to AI alone because it can be wrong too; it can point you to where to look, but a person confirms with a source.
openers.lookFor: Groups justify placing judgment and fact-checking with humans and explain how they would check anything AI contributes.
openers.next: Students will co-create a piece with AI and log every suggestion they keep, change, or reject.

openers.title: The Post From Ninth Grade
openers.prompt: Imagine a scholarship committee or a future boss searches your name. They find a joke you posted in ninth grade that made fun of someone. Write what you would want them to understand, and one thing you would do now to shape what people find.
openers.teacher: Students write privately for three minutes; volunteers share only the second part. Ask: "Is deleting enough? Where else might that post still exist?"
openers.lookFor: Students name concrete actions, such as reviewing old posts, adjusting privacy settings, apologizing, or building a positive record, and recognize screenshots and reposts can outlast deletion.
openers.next: Students will build a personal digital safety plan and explain it to a family member.

openers.title: Stand for the Streak
openers.prompt: Stand if it's true for you, then sit. 1) I have opened an app just to keep a streak alive. 2) I have lost track of time on autoplay. 3) I have turned off a notification on purpose. 4) I have a time of day that's screen-free. Then set one small goal for this week.
openers.teacher: Read each statement and pause; nobody explains unless they volunteer. Close with a 60-second private write: one goal and how you'll know you met it. Ask: "Which of these was designed by the app, and which was your choice?"
openers.lookFor: Goals are specific and measurable, such as turning off one app's notifications or keeping phones out of the bedroom on school nights.
openers.next: Check goals at the end of the week and adjust; students who want to go deeper can audit a notification setting at home.

openers.title: The Summary That Drifted
openers.prompt: From a fictional 1911 letter: "The mill fire began after dark. Mr. Okafor and the Ruiz family carried water until dawn. Some say a lantern tipped, but no one saw it." An AI summary: "The mill fire started at 6 p.m. when a lantern tipped over. The mayor led the rescue." Which change matters most?
openers.teacher: Students vote with fingers, then partners defend their pick. Ask: "If you only read the summary, what would you get wrong on a test or in a paper?"
openers.answer: All of them. The summary invents a specific time, turns an unconfirmed rumor into a cause, and replaces the neighbors who helped with a mayor who is not in the letter. AI summaries can save time, but you still have to compare them with the original.
openers.lookFor: Students cite the exact words in the letter that the summary changed or erased.
openers.next: Students will read the full fictional letter and catch every change an AI summary makes.

openers.title: What the Ads Think You Like
openers.prompt: On a device and account you already use, find the ad settings or "why am I seeing this ad" page. Look at the interests it has guessed about you. How accurate is the profile?
openers.teacher: Give students four minutes to look; anyone without an account or device pairs up or watches you walk through a school demo account on the projector. Students vote with fingers and share one surprising guess only if they want to. Ask: "What did you do online that might have led to that guess, and will you change any setting?"
openers.lookFor: Students connect a specific guessed interest to something they did online and decide whether to change a setting.
openers.next: Students will look deeper at how app design and data shape what they see in feeds and ads.
